Nempe, ut asserit Beda: Hoc in vita hac inter electos et reprobos solet distare, quod electi tanto minus gaudiis delectantur caducis, quanto plus perpetua gaudia præstolantur. Reprobi vero hic patriam habent, quia terrenis et carnalibus magis quam spiritualibus inhiant. Ideo post hanc vitam in perpetuum relegantur exilium.
paras.en: Let us therefore despise carnal affections and their effects, kisses and embraces, games, jests, loud laughter, pleasures, vanities and base consolations; let us not fix our mind on the things of this world, but hasten with all our heart to the fatherland of eternal happiness: just as pilgrims do not seek to linger or take their pleasure on the way, but hasten and aspire to their fatherland. This concerns every Christian, since the Saviour says: [[Luke 6:24|woe to you that are rich|Væ vobis divitibus]], [[Luke 6:24|for you have your consolation|qui habetis consolationem vestram]]; [[Luke 6:25|Woe to you that are filled: for you shall hunger. Woe to you that now laugh: for you shall mourn|væ vobis qui saturati estis, quia esurietis; væ vobis qui ridetis nunc, quia plorabitis]] [Denis has only *plorabitis*, you shall weep]. Hence it is set down to the Galatians: [[Gal 5:24|And they that are Christ's have crucified their flesh, with the vices and concupiscences.|Qui autem sunt Christi, carnem suam crucifixerunt cum vitiis et concupiscentiis]] So in food, drink, sleep, clothing and the other things that concern the body, let us seek not superfluity or pleasure but necessity, as the Vessel of election [that is, Paul] exhorts: [[1 Tim 6:8|having food and wherewith to be covered, with these we are content|Habentes alimenta et quibus tegamur, his contenti simus]]. For which reason the Wise Man prays: [[Prov 30:8|give me only the necessaries of life|Tribue tantum victui meo necessaria]]. Since, then, we are marked with a kingly and priestly name, let us disdain to be put under the yoke of the vices, lest we fall away from the nobility of grace bestowed on us and from the sublimity of the glory promised us. For, as Bede says: In this life the elect and the reprobate commonly differ in this, that the elect take the less delight in passing joys the more they look for everlasting joys; but the reprobate have their fatherland here, since they crave earthly and carnal things more than spiritual ones. Therefore after this life they are banished into everlasting exile.

paras.t: Conversationem vestram inter gentes habentes bonam, id est virtuosam et exemplarem, ut in eo quod detrectant de vobis tanquam de malefactoribus. Carnales enim et impii vituperant justos, et detrahunt eis quorum virtutes assequi nolunt, quemadmodum in Proverbiis legitur: Ambulans recto itinere et timens Deum, despicitur ab eo qui infami graditur via. Et rursus Salomon contestatur: Viri sanguinum oderunt simplicem. Job quoque ait: Deridetur justi simplicitas. Et in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: Abominatio superbo humilitas. Ex bonis operibus vos considerantes, id est opera vestra evidenter excellenterque virtuosa pensantes, et ex eis ipsa veritate convicti, bonos vos esse recognoscentes, glorificent Deum in die visitationis, id est, Deum in suis servis collaudent, atque ex puritate et eminentia vitæ servorum, sanctitatem Domini pensent ac fateantur, in die visitationis, quum corda eorum irradiaverit ac visitaverit gratia Spiritus Sancti, dum scilicet ex prædicta consideratione compuncti fuerint et conversi; vel in die judicii, quum viderint remunerationem justorum, et velint nolint, fateantur sanctitatem atque justitiam Dei. Hoc est quod Christus docet ac jubet: Sic luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, ut videant bona facta vestra, et glorificent Patrem vestrum qui in cœlis est.
paras.en: [[2:12|Having your conversation good among the Gentiles|Conversationem vestram inter gentes habentes bonam]], that is, virtuous and exemplary, [[2:12|that whereas they speak against you as evildoers|ut in eo quod detrectant de vobis tanquam de malefactoribus]]. For carnal and ungodly men revile the just, and detract those whose virtues they will not strive after, as we read in Proverbs: [[Prov 14:2|He that walketh in the right way, and feareth God, is despised by him that goeth by an infamous way.|Ambulans recto itinere et timens Deum, despicitur ab eo qui infami graditur via]] And again Solomon testifies: [[Prov 29:10|Bloodthirsty men hate the upright|Viri sanguinum oderunt simplicem]]. Job too says: [[Job 12:4|the simplicity of the just man is laughed to scorn|Deridetur justi simplicitas]]. And in Ecclesiasticus it is written: [[Ecclus 13:24|humility is an abomination to the proud|Abominatio superbo humilitas]]. [[2:12|by the good works which they shall behold in you|Ex bonis operibus vos considerantes]], that is, weighing your works, plainly and excellently virtuous, and convinced by them through the very truth, recognising that you are good, they may [[2:12|glorify God in the day of visitation|glorificent Deum in die visitationis]]: that is, that they may praise God in his servants, and from the purity and eminence of the servants' life weigh and confess the holiness of the Lord, [[2:12|in the day of visitation|in die visitationis]], when the grace of the Holy Ghost has shone upon their hearts and visited them, that is, when they have been pricked to the heart by this consideration and converted; or on the day of judgment, when they see the reward of the just and, willing or unwilling, confess the holiness and justice of God. This is what Christ teaches and commands: [[Matt 5:16|So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven|Sic luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, ut videant bona facta vestra, et glorificent Patrem vestrum qui in cœlis est]].

paras.t: Proximis enim debemus bonum exemplum, et Deo conscientiam mundam. Quia tenemur proximos spiritualiter semper diligere, idcirco tenemur eorum scandalizationem vitare, et ipsos ædificare. Deum quoque tenemur pro viribus honorare in nobis ipsis ac aliis. Ideo debemus alios pro posse ad Dei venerationem verbis et factis inducere: quod agendo, ipsum sanctificare magnificareque dicimur. Qui vero alios scandalizant, et impie conversantur, Deum, quantum in ipsis est, vilificare et maculare feruntur. Propter quod Deus per Prophetam ait Judæis: Commaculastis nomen sanctum meum; et iterum, Polluistis nomen meum in gentibus.
paras.en: For we owe our neighbours a good example, and God a clean conscience. Since we are bound always to love our neighbours spiritually, we are bound to avoid scandalizing them and to edify them. We are bound also to honour God as far as we can, in ourselves and in others. Therefore we ought, as far as we are able, to lead others by words and deeds to the worship of God; and in doing this we are said to sanctify and magnify him. But those who scandalize others and live ungodly lives are said, as far as in them lies, to cheapen and defile God. For which reason God says to the Jews through the Prophet: You [[Jer 34:16|have defiled my name|Commaculastis nomen sanctum meum]] [Denis has *my holy name*]; and again: My name [[Ezech 36:22|you have profaned among the nations|Polluistis nomen meum in gentibus]].

paras.t: Denique omnia ista, videlicet a carnalibus desideriis abstinere, exemplariter conversari, Deum in se ac aliis honorare, ad prælatos et sacerdotes, ad religiosos et prædicatores potissime pertinent.
paras.en: Lastly, all these things, namely to refrain from carnal desires, to live as an example, and to honour God in oneself and in others, concern above all prelates and priests, religious and preachers.

2.title: EXPLANATIO RESIDUI HUJUS CAPITULI SECUNDI : SUBJECTI IGITUR ESTOTE.
2.title_en: Explanation of the rest of this second chapter: Be ye subject therefore.

paras.t: HUCUSQUE introduxit sacratissimus Petrus documenta, ad universos fideles spectantia; nunc certis personis ac diversis suppositis, speciales tradit doctrinas ac jussiones, quatenus unusquisque secundum suæ exigentiam vocationis ambulet digne Deo. Diversi namque ad diversa sunt obligati, secundum varias conditiones et proprietates quæ eis conveniunt.
paras.en: Up to this point the most holy Peter has set out teachings that concern all the faithful; now he gives special teachings and commands to certain persons and to various subjects, so that each one, according to what his vocation requires[[Eph 4:1||]], may [[Col 1:10|walk worthy of God|ambulet digne Deo]]. For different people are bound to different things, according to the various conditions and properties that befit them.

paras.t: Itaque ait: Subjecti igitur estote omni humanæ creaturæ propter Deum. Hoc dupliciter explanatur: Primo, per omnem humanam creaturam intelligendo omnem hominem. Nam omnis homo, in quantum ad Dei imaginem factus est, ad æternam felicitatem creatus, et Christi passione redemptus, aliquo modo est honorandus, præsertim quia humana natura in Dei Unigenito ad esse personale Verbi æterni assumpta est in unitatem personæ. Quilibet etiam, secundum aliquam sui considerationem, potest se alio quolibet, secundum aliquam illius considerationem, reputare inferiorem. Sicque alteri cuilibet se potest ex humilitate aliquo modo subjicere: et hoc, propter Deum, id est propter ipsius honorem, et quia hoc complacet ei, et quoniam ejus imago resplendet in homine. Hinc loquitur Paulus: Honore invicem prævenientes; et rursus, Per caritatem servite in invicem. Ad Philippenses quoque: Nihil, inquit, agatis per contentionem, neque per inanem gloriam, sed per humilitatem superiores sibi invicem arbitrantes. Hinc et Christus ait: Si ego lavi pedes vestros, Dominus et magister, et vos debetis alter alterius lavare pedes; et alibi, Qui major est vestrum, sit vester minister. Propterea quoque in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: Quanto magnus es, humilia te in omnibus, et coram Deo invenies gratiam.
paras.en: So he says: [[2:13|Be ye subject therefore to every human creature for God's sake|Subjecti igitur estote omni humanæ creaturæ propter Deum]]. This is explained in two ways. First, by understanding *every human creature* as every man. For every man, in so far as he was made to the image of God[[Gen 1:27||]], created for eternal happiness and redeemed by the passion of Christ, is in some way to be honoured; above all because human nature, in the only-begotten Son of God, was assumed into the personal being of the eternal Word, into unity of person. Again, anyone, considering himself in some respect, can reckon himself inferior to anyone else, considering that other in some respect. And so out of humility he can in some way subject himself to anyone else; and this [[2:13|for God's sake|propter Deum]], that is, for His honour, and because this is pleasing to Him, and because His image shines forth in man. Hence Paul says: [[Rom 12:10|with honour preventing one another|Honore invicem prævenientes]] [that is, going before one another in showing honour]; and again, [[Gal 5:13|by charity of the spirit serve one another|Per caritatem servite in invicem]]. And to the Philippians: [[Phil 2:3|Let nothing be done|Nihil]], he says, [[Phil 2:3|through contention: neither by vain glory. But in humility, let each esteem others better than themselves|agatis per contentionem, neque per inanem gloriam, sed per humilitatem superiores sibi invicem arbitrantes]]. Hence Christ too says: [[John 13:14|If then I being your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; you also ought to wash one another's feet|Si ego lavi pedes vestros, Dominus et magister, et vos debetis alter alterius lavare pedes]]; and elsewhere, [[Matt 20:26|whosoever is the greater among you, let him be your minister|Qui major est vestrum, sit vester minister]] [Denis's wording begins as in Matt 23:11, He that is the greatest among you]. Therefore it is also written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 3:20|The greater thou art, the more humble thyself in all things, and thou shalt find grace before God|Quanto magnus es, humilia te in omnibus, et coram Deo invenies gratiam]].

paras.t: Secundo exponitur, intelligendo per omnem humanam creaturam, omnem præsidentem. Sicque Beda exponit, dicendo: Omni humanæ creaturæ, dicit, Omni hominum dignitati, omni principatui. Quam expositionem sequitur Glossa. Illis ergo debet se omnis inferior subdere propter Deum, in quantum ejus repræsentant personam, seu ejus vicarii sunt in terra, et quoniam Deus id exigit, atque ut bonum æternum consequamur finaliter pro beatitudine objectali, hoc est propter Deum fruitive ac æternaliter possidendum, et item propter eum nunc honorandum, ut scilicet eum in suis veneremur ministris, quibus locutus est: Qui vos audit, me audit; et qui vos spernit, me spernit. Ideo ad Romanos dicitur: Omnis anima potestatibus sublimioribus subdita sit: non enim est potestas nisi a Deo. Itaque qui resistit potestati, Dei ordinationi resistit; qui autem resistunt, ipsi sibi damnationem acquirunt.
paras.en: Secondly, it is explained by understanding *every human creature* as everyone in authority. Thus Bede explains it, saying: [[2:13|To every human creature|Omni humanæ creaturæ]], he says: to every dignity among men, to every principality. The Gloss follows this explanation. To these, then, every inferior ought to subject himself [[2:13|for God's sake|propter Deum]], in so far as they represent His person, or are His vicars on earth, and because God requires it; and so that we may finally attain the eternal good as our objective beatitude [that is, God himself as the object in whom beatitude consists], that is, for the sake of possessing God by fruition and eternally; and likewise for the sake of honouring Him now, namely so that we may reverence Him in His ministers, to whom He said: [[Luke 10:16|He that heareth you heareth me: and he that despiseth you despiseth me|Qui vos audit, me audit; et qui vos spernit, me spernit]]. Therefore it is said to the Romans: [[Rom 13:1|Let every soul be subject to higher powers. For there is no power but from God|Omnis anima potestatibus sublimioribus subdita sit: non enim est potestas nisi a Deo]]. [[Rom 13:2|Therefore, he that resisteth the power resisteth the ordinance of God. And they that resist purchase to themselves damnation.|Itaque qui resistit potestati, Dei ordinationi resistit; qui autem resistunt, ipsi sibi damnationem acquirunt]]

paras.t: Sive regi quasi prævenienti: id est, regi tanquam eminenti principi debent se subditi ejus subjicere, eique obedire in his quæ cathedram suam concernunt, seu suum respiciunt principatum, quæ utique non sunt contra Dei honorem, nec contra bonum justitiæ: sive ducibus tanquam ab eo missis: id est, inferioribus principibus officiatisque regum debet se homo subjicere, et eis parere in his quæ eis rite commissa sunt, nec eorum potestatem seu jurisdictionem excedunt. Idcirco subjungitur: ad vindictam malefactorum, laudem vero bonorum, id est ad hoc a rege directis, ut pravorum vitia ulciscantur, justisque laudem ac dignam mercedem rependant. Ad hoc enim mittendi sunt, quamvis frequenter ad alia dirigantur agenda, quia multoties reges potestate abutuntur collata: quæ tamen eis collata est ut malos per pœnas coerceant, peccata exstirpent, subditos ad virtutes inducant, et bonum conservent commune. Propter quod ad Romanos fertur: Principes non sunt timori boni operis, sed mali. Vis autem non timere potestatem? Fac bonum, et habebis laudem ex illa: Dei enim minister est tibi in bonum. Si autem male egeris, time: non enim sine causa gladium portat. Dei enim minister est, vindex in iram ei qui male agit.
paras.en: [[2:13|whether it be to the king as excelling|Sive regi quasi prævenienti]] [Denis reads *prævenienti*, "going before", where the Vulgate has *præcellenti*, "excelling"]: that is, his subjects ought to subject themselves to the king as to the pre-eminent prince, and obey him in those things that concern his seat of authority, or pertain to his rule, which are certainly not against the honour of God nor against the good of justice; [[2:14|Or to governors as sent by him|sive ducibus tanquam ab eo missis]]: that is, a man ought to subject himself to the lesser princes and officers of kings, and obey them in the things that have been duly committed to them and do not go beyond their power or jurisdiction. Therefore it is added: [[2:14|for the punishment of evildoers and for the praise of the good|ad vindictam malefactorum, laudem vero bonorum]], that is, directed by the king to this end, that they may punish the vices of the wicked and render praise and a worthy reward to the just. For this is what they are to be sent for, although they are often directed to do other things, because kings many times abuse the power conferred on them: which was nevertheless conferred on them so that they might restrain the wicked by punishments, root out sins, lead their subjects to the virtues and preserve the common good. Wherefore it is said to the Romans: [[Rom 13:3|princes are not a terror to the good work, but to the evil. Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power? Do that which is good: and thou shalt have praise from the same|Principes non sunt timori boni operis, sed mali. Vis autem non timere potestatem? Fac bonum, et habebis laudem ex illa]]: [[Rom 13:4|For he is God's minister to thee, for good. But if thou do that which is evil, fear: for he beareth not the sword in vain. For he is God's minister: an avenger to execute wrath upon him that doth evil|Dei enim minister est tibi in bonum. Si autem male egeris, time: non enim sine causa gladium portat. Dei enim minister est, vindex in iram ei qui male agit]].

paras.t: Quia sic est voluntas, id est doctrina ac jussio, Dei, ut benefacientes, id est prælato modo obedientes, obmutescere faciatis imprudentium hominum ignorantiam, id est, perversos ac perfidos seu impios præsidentes per vestram obedientiam virtuosamque vitam reprimatis a detractione ac ceteris vitiis quæ inciderent, si vos inobedientes terrenæ potestati conspicerent. Unde bene agendo, subtrahitis eis obloquendi materiam, et vestra bonitate ac sapientia eorum improbitatem insipientiamque convincitis, quantum in vobis est, ita quod rationabiliter contradicere nequeunt. Quamobrem ad Titum loquitur Paulus: In omnibus teipsum præbe exemplum bonorum operum; verbum sanum sit et irreprehensibile, ut is qui ex adverso est, vereatur, nihil mali habens loqui de nobis. Ad Philippenses quoque: Sitis, inquit, sine querela, simplices filii Dei, in medio nationis pravæ atque perversæ, inter quos lucetis sicut luminaria mundi, verbum vitæ continentes. Et alibi: Nemini dantes ullam offensionem, ut non vituperetur ministerium nostrum.
paras.en: [[2:15|For so is the will|Quia sic est voluntas]], that is, the teaching and command, of God, [[2:15|that by doing well|ut benefacientes]], that is, by obeying in the way described, [[2:15|you may put to silence the ignorance of foolish men|obmutescere faciatis imprudentium hominum ignorantiam]]: that is, that by your obedience and virtuous life you may restrain perverse and faithless or impious rulers from detraction and the other vices into which they would fall if they saw you disobedient to earthly power. Hence, by doing well you take from them matter for speaking against you, and by your goodness and wisdom you convict their wickedness and folly, as far as in you lies, so that they cannot reasonably gainsay you. Wherefore Paul says to Titus: [[Tit 2:7|In all things shew thyself an example of good works|In omnibus teipsum præbe exemplum bonorum operum]]; [[Tit 2:8|The sound word that can not be blamed: that he who is on the contrary part may be afraid, having no evil to say of us|verbum sanum sit et irreprehensibile, ut is qui ex adverso est, vereatur, nihil mali habens loqui de nobis]]. And to the Philippians: Be ye, he says, [[Phil 2:15|blameless and sincere children of God|sine querela, simplices filii Dei]], [[Phil 2:15|in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation: among whom you shine as lights in the world|in medio nationis pravæ atque perversæ, inter quos lucetis sicut luminaria mundi]], [[Phil 2:16|Holding forth the word of life|verbum vitæ continentes]]. And elsewhere: [[2 Cor 6:3|Giving no offence to any man, that our ministry be not blamed|Nemini dantes ullam offensionem, ut non vituperetur ministerium nostrum]].

paras.t: Quasi liberi, id est, ea quæ dicta sunt, adimplete, quasi vere liberi libertate spirituali, quæ est immunitas a jugo diaboli et servitute peccati, a quibus per Christi gratiam estis erepti. Propter quod ipsemet Christus de se ipso fatetur: Si Filius vos liberaverit, vere liberi eritis. Et non quasi velamen habentes malitiæ libertatem. Ordo verborum et sensus sunt: Non quasi habentes libertatem, velamen malitiæ, hoc est, libertatem præfatam non vertatis nec assumatis in velamen, seu excusationem aut palliationem erroris aut pravitatis, putando quod ideo non debeatis esse subjecti terrenis aut infidelibus dominis, quia a Christo constituti estis in libertate. Hæc enim libertas prædictæ subjectioni non derogat, sed servituti peccati atque diaboli. Quidam vero dixerunt, se non obligatos dare tributum, aut perfidis terrenisve principibus subjacere, quoniam filii Dei et liberi facti fuerunt per Christi Baptismum. Quod fuit erroneum, quum dicat Salvator: Reddite quæ sunt Cæsaris, Cæsari; et quæ sunt Dei, Deo. De hac libertate dicta sunt multa super illud Jacobi, Qui autem perspexerit in lege perfectæ libertatis, etc. Sed sicut servi Dei, id est sicut Deo veraciter subditi. Deus namque requirit ut potestati ab ipso collatæ recte obediatur.
paras.en: [[2:16|As free|Quasi liberi]], that is, fulfil what has been said as men truly free with spiritual freedom, which is immunity from the yoke of the devil and the servitude of sin, from which you have been rescued by the grace of Christ. Wherefore Christ himself says of himself: [[John 8:36|If therefore the son shall make you free, you shall be free indeed|Si Filius vos liberaverit, vere liberi eritis]] [the margin gives John viii, 30]. [[2:16|and not as making liberty a cloak for malice|Et non quasi velamen habentes malitiæ libertatem]]. The order of the words and the sense are: not as having liberty as a cloak of malice; that is, do not turn or take up the aforesaid liberty into a cloak, or an excuse or palliation, for error or wickedness, thinking that you need not therefore be subject to earthly or unbelieving masters because you have been set in liberty by Christ. For this liberty does not take away from the subjection spoken of, but from the servitude of sin and of the devil. Some, indeed, have said that they were not bound to pay tribute, or to be subject to faithless or earthly princes, because they had been made sons of God and free through the Baptism of Christ. This was erroneous, since the Saviour says: [[Matt 22:21|Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar's; and to God, the things that are God's|Reddite quæ sunt Cæsaris, Cæsari; et quæ sunt Dei, Deo]] [the margin gives Matth. xxi, 21]. Much has been said of this liberty on that passage of James, [[Jas 1:25|he that hath looked into the perfect law of liberty|Qui autem perspexerit in lege perfectæ libertatis]], etc. [[2:16|but as the servants of God|Sed sicut servi Dei]], that is, as truly subject to God. For God requires that the power He has conferred be rightly obeyed.

paras.t: Denique libertatem suam in velamen assumunt malitiæ, qui tanto irrefrenatius peccant, quo minus humanæ potestati subduntur: ut pravi prælati principesque iniqui faciunt, in quibus non est timor Dei, nec pensant illud Sapientiæ: Altissimus cito et horrende apparebit vobis, quia judicium durissimum in his qui præsunt, fiet. Qui autem vere sapientes et timorati sunt, tanto virtuosius conversantur, quo minus se vident hominibus subditos, ac magis divino judicio reservatos, quo etiam pluribus præsident, atque pro pluribus daturi sunt rationem. Hinc loquitur Paulus: Vos in libertatem vocati estis, fratres: tantum, ne libertatem in occasionem carnis detis.
paras.en: Further, those take up their liberty as a cloak for malice who sin the more unbridledly the less they are subject to human power: as wicked prelates and unjust princes do, in whom there is no fear of God, and who do not weigh that saying of Wisdom: [[Wis 6:6|Horribly and speedily will he appear to you: for a most severe judgment shall be for them that bear rule.|Altissimus cito et horrende apparebit vobis, quia judicium durissimum in his qui præsunt, fiet]] [Denis's text begins *Altissimus*, "the Most High", taken from v. 4]. But those who are truly wise and God-fearing live the more virtuously the less they see themselves subject to men and the more reserved to the divine judgment, and the more people they rule over and must render account for. Hence Paul says: [[Gal 5:13|you, brethren, have been called unto liberty. Only make not liberty an occasion to the flesh|Vos in libertatem vocati estis, fratres: tantum, ne libertatem in occasionem carnis detis]].

paras.t: Omnes honorate, in quantum ad Dei imaginem sunt creati, et propter alias rationes jam tactas. Impii tamen secundum quod tales, sunt contemnendi, sicut de justo ait Propheta: Ad nihilum deductus est in conspectu ejus malignus. Et in Proverbiis habetur: Abominantur justi virum impium. Verumtamen judicando de aliis, an sint tales, necesse est grandi uti discretione atque custodia. Fraternitatem diligite, id est fratres seu proximos, præsertim Christifideles ac virtuosos, quum asserat Christus: Hoc est præceptum meum, ut diligatis invicem sicut dilexi vos. Deum timete filiali timore, ne eum offendatis, inhonoretis, et ne ab eo separemini, quum ipse sit summum et incomparabile bonum. Propter quod ait Salvator: Eum timete qui habet potestatem corpus et animam perdere in gehennam. Et apud Isaiam inducitur: Dominum exercituum sanctificate; ipse pavor vester, et ipse terror vester. Hoc sanctus Job eminenter implevit, qui fassus est: Deus solus est, et cogitationem ejus nemo avertere potest; idcirco considerans eum, timore sollicitor. Et rursus: Semper, inquit, quasi tumentes super me fluctus timui Deum. Et certe, si consideremus quam terribilis sit Deus in consiliis super filios hominum, quam incomprehensibilia sint judicia ejus, quam horrendum sit incidere in manus ejus, timebimus cum timore ingenti, incomparabili, incessanti. Regem, id est terrenum principem, honorificate, ei obediendo in his quæ sui sunt officii. Quemadmodum autem Deus honorandus est cultu latriæ, sic homines honorificentia duliæ.
paras.en: [[2:17|Honour all men|Omnes honorate]], in so far as they are created to the image of God[[Gen 1:27||]], and for the other reasons already touched on. Yet the wicked, as such, are to be despised, as the Prophet says of the just man: [[Ps 14:4|In his sight the malignant is brought to nothing|Ad nihilum deductus est in conspectu ejus malignus]]. And in Proverbs we have: [[Prov 29:27|The just abhor a wicked man|Abominantur justi virum impium]] [the margin gives Prov. xxiv, 27]. Nevertheless, in judging of others whether they are such, great discretion and caution must be used. [[2:17|Love the brotherhood|Fraternitatem diligite]], that is, the brethren or neighbours, especially the faithful of Christ and the virtuous, since Christ declares: [[John 15:12|This is my commandment, that you love one another, as I have loved you|Hoc est præceptum meum, ut diligatis invicem sicut dilexi vos]]. [[2:17|Fear God|Deum timete]] with a filial fear, lest you offend Him or dishonour Him, and lest you be separated from Him, since He is the highest and incomparable good. Wherefore the Saviour says: [[Matt 10:28|fear him that can destroy both soul and body in hell|Eum timete qui habet potestatem corpus et animam perdere in gehennam]]. And in Isaias it is set down: [[Is 8:13|Sanctify the Lord of hosts himself: and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread|Dominum exercituum sanctificate; ipse pavor vester, et ipse terror vester]]. This holy Job fulfilled eminently, who confessed: [[Job 23:13|he is alone, and no man can turn away his thought|Deus solus est, et cogitationem ejus nemo avertere potest]]; therefore [[Job 23:15|when I consider him, I am made pensive with fear|considerans eum, timore sollicitor]]. And again: [[Job 31:23|I have always feared God as waves swelling over me|Semper, inquit, quasi tumentes super me fluctus timui Deum]], he says. And certainly, if we consider how God is [[Ps 65:5|terrible in his counsels over the sons of men|terribilis sit Deus in consiliis super filios hominum]], [[Rom 11:33|How incomprehensible are his judgments|quam incomprehensibilia sint judicia ejus]], and how it is [[Heb 10:31|a fearful thing to fall into the hands|horrendum sit incidere in manus]] of him, we shall fear with a fear immense, incomparable, unceasing. [[2:17|the king|Regem]], that is, the earthly prince, [[2:17|Honour|honorificate]], by obeying him in those things that belong to his office. And as God is to be honoured with the worship of latria [that is, the worship due to God alone], so men are to be honoured with the reverence of dulia [that is, the honour paid to creatures for their excellence].

paras.t: Hæc autem jam dicta ab exordio hujus articuli, secundum Bedam intelliguntur de Christianis liberis, servos sub se habentibus, tamen principi terreno et ducibus ejus subjectis. Quæ autem sequuntur, exponenda sunt de servis dumtaxat. Servi, o vos ministri conducticii sive empticii, subditi estote in omni timore, id est perfecta et filiali formidine, dominis temporalibus, non tantum bonis, id est virtuosis interius, et modestis, id est ordinatis et exemplaribus foris, sed etiam dyscolis, id est indisciplinatis et iniquis, quamdiu non jubent ultra quam se extendit eorum jurisdictio sive dominium. Unicuique namque obediendum est in his quæ præsidentiæ suæ respiciunt cathedram.
paras.en: What has been said from the beginning of this article is understood, according to Bede, of free Christians who have servants under them, yet are subject to the earthly prince and his governors. But what follows is to be explained of servants only. [[2:18|Servants|Servi]], O you ministers, hired or bought, [[2:18|be subject|subditi estote]] [[2:18|with all fear|in omni timore]], that is, with perfect and filial awe, [[2:18|to your masters|dominis]] of this world, [[2:18|not only to the good|non tantum bonis]], that is, the virtuous within, [[2:18|and gentle|et modestis]], that is, the orderly and exemplary without, [[2:18|but also to the froward|sed etiam dyscolis]] [the Greek word *dyscolus* means "hard to please", "perverse"], that is, the undisciplined and wicked, so long as they do not command beyond the reach of their jurisdiction or lordship. For everyone is to be obeyed in the things that pertain to the seat of his authority.

paras.t: Sed his objici potest illud Proverbiorum, Qui timet hominem, cito corruet; et quod rursus Salomon fatur: Fili, honora Deum, et valebis; præter eum vero ne timueris alienum. Ex quibus sequi videtur, quod non sit hominibus cum timore obediendum aut serviendum. — Et respondendum, quod timere hominem secundum se, non per respectum ad Deum et secundum ordinem æquitatis, vituperabile exsistit, et diversorum occasio vitiorum. Homines vero timere in Deo, secundum Deum, et propter Deum, in quantum sunt ejus vicarii, aut aliquid divinæ proprietatis participantes, est laudandum. Sicque intendit princeps Apostolorum, ut dominis temporalibus obediatur cum timore Dei filiali et casto, non cum timore carnali, humano. Illud enim meritorium est, non istud. Omnia quippe cum hujusmodi timore Dei agenda sunt, ne scilicet eum in aliquo offendamus. Unde hanc ipsam sententiam Paulus ad Ephesios clarius exprimit, dicens: Servi, obedite dominis carnalibus cum timore et tremore, in simplicitate cordis vestri, sicut Christo: non ad oculum servientes, quasi hominibus placentes; sed ut servi Christi, facientes voluntatem Dei ex animo, cum bona voluntate, servientes sicut Domino, et non quasi hominibus: scientes quoniam unusquisque quod fecerit bonum, hoc percipiet a Domino, sive servus, sive liber. Ex quibus ostenditur, quod temporalibus dominis obediendum ac serviendum est principaliter atque finaliter propter cœlestem felicitatem et Dei honorem, ex caritate, cum divino timore.
paras.en: But against this may be objected that saying of Proverbs, [[Prov 29:25|He that feareth man shall quickly fall|Qui timet hominem, cito corruet]]; and what Solomon says again: Son, honour God, and thou shalt be strong; but beside him fear no stranger[[Prov 7:1||]] [this sentence stands at the end of Prov 7:1 in the Vulgate; the Douay-Rheims text in the app breaks off there after "Son,"]. From these it seems to follow that men are not to be obeyed or served with fear. The answer is that to fear a man in himself, not with respect to God and according to the order of equity, is blameworthy and the occasion of various vices. But to fear men in God, according to God and for God's sake, in so far as they are His vicars or share in something of the divine property, is praiseworthy. And so the prince of the Apostles means that temporal masters are to be obeyed with the filial and chaste fear of God, not with a carnal, human fear. For the former is meritorious, not the latter. For all things are to be done with this kind of fear of God, namely lest we offend Him in anything. Hence Paul expresses this very sentence more clearly to the Ephesians, saying: [[Eph 6:5|Servants, be obedient to them that are your lords according to the flesh, with fear and trembling, in the simplicity of your heart, as to Christ|Servi, obedite dominis carnalibus cum timore et tremore, in simplicitate cordis vestri, sicut Christo]]: [[Eph 6:6|Not serving to the eye, as it were pleasing men: but, as the servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart|non ad oculum servientes, quasi hominibus placentes; sed ut servi Christi, facientes voluntatem Dei ex animo]], [[Eph 6:7|With a good will serving, as to the Lord, and not to men|cum bona voluntate, servientes sicut Domino, et non quasi hominibus]]: [[Eph 6:8|Knowing that whatsoever good thing any man shall do, the same shall he receive from the Lord, whether he be bond or free|scientes quoniam unusquisque quod fecerit bonum, hoc percipiet a Domino, sive servus, sive liber]]. From this it is shown that temporal masters are to be obeyed and served principally and finally for the sake of heavenly happiness and the honour of God, out of charity, with the fear of God.

paras.t: Deinde subditur ratio, cur etiam sit dyscolis dominis propter Deum formidolose obediendum. Hæc est enim gratia, id est res Deo grata, accepta et gratiosa, si propter conscientiam Dei, id est propter bonam coram Deo conscientiam habendam, sustinet quis tristitias, id est persecutiones, pœnas, injurias, quæ solent inferre tristitias patienti, patiens injuste, id est eas æquanimiter tolerans absque suis demeritis. Quæ est enim gratia, id est, quod meritum vobis debetur, vel quid Deo acceptum peragitis, si peccantes et colaphizati suffertis, id est, si correctionem pro vestris peccatis patimini a dominis vestris? quasi dicat, Nihil: quia de jure pœna debetur culpæ. Sed si bene facientes, patienter sustinetis tribulationes vobis injuste inflictas, hæc est gratia, id est res valde accepta, apud Deum. Talis namque sustinentia, satisfactoria est pro peccatis in Deum commissis, et meritoria gratiæ amplioris in via, ac gloriæ plenioris in patria. Per eam quoque conformantur homines Christo injustissime passo.
paras.en: Next is given the reason why even froward masters are to be obeyed with fear for God's sake. [[2:19|For this is thankworthy|Hæc est enim gratia]] [*gratia*, "grace" or "favour": that which is pleasing], that is, a thing pleasing to God, acceptable and gracious, [[2:19|if, for conscience towards God|si propter conscientiam Dei]], that is, for the sake of keeping a good conscience before God, [[2:19|a man endure sorrows|sustinet quis tristitias]], that is, persecutions, punishments, injuries, which usually bring sorrow to the one who suffers them, [[2:19|suffering wrongfully|patiens injuste]], that is, bearing them with equanimity without having deserved them. [[2:20|For what glory is it|Quæ est enim gratia]] [Denis reads *gratia* here too, where the Vulgate has *gloria*], that is, what merit is owed to you, or what do you accomplish that is acceptable to God, [[2:20|if, committing sin and being buffeted for it, you endure|si peccantes et colaphizati suffertis]], that is, if you suffer correction from your masters for your sins? As if he said: none; because by right punishment is owed to fault. [[2:20|But if doing well you suffer patiently|Sed si bene facientes, patienter sustinetis]] the tribulations unjustly inflicted on you, [[2:20|this is thankworthy|hæc est gratia]], that is, a thing very acceptable, [[2:20|before God|apud Deum]]. For such endurance makes satisfaction for the sins committed against God, and merits fuller grace on the way and fuller glory in the fatherland. By it, too, men are conformed to Christ, who suffered most unjustly.

paras.t: Ideo subditur: In hoc enim vocati estis, id est ad fidem et legem Evangelii gratiose adducti, ut sitis in adversitatibus injuste inflictis patientes. Propter quod Christus ait discipulis: Si me persecuti sunt, et vos persequentur, quia non est servus major domino suo. Et denuo protestatur: Sicut dilexit me Pater, et ego dilexi vos. Tanquam dicat: Sicut a Patre diligor, et nihilo minus adversis in sæculo isto affligor; ita vos diligo, et tamen tribulationibus vos expono. Hinc Paulus fatetur: Omnes qui volunt pie vivere in Christo, persecutionem patientur.
paras.en: Therefore it is added: [[2:21|For unto this are you called|In hoc enim vocati estis]], that is, graciously brought to the faith and law of the Gospel, so that you may be patient in adversities unjustly inflicted. Wherefore Christ says to his disciples: [[John 15:20|If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you|Si me persecuti sunt, et vos persequentur]], because [[John 15:20|The servant is not greater than his master|non est servus major domino suo]]. And again he declares: [[John 15:9|As the Father hath loved me, I also have loved you|Sicut dilexit me Pater, et ego dilexi vos]]. As if he said: As I am loved by the Father, and none the less am afflicted with adversities in this world, so I love you, and yet I expose you to tribulations. Hence Paul declares: [[2 Tim 3:12|all that will live godly in Christ|Omnes qui volunt pie vivere in Christo]], [[2 Tim 3:12|shall suffer persecution|persecutionem patientur]] [the margin gives II Tim. ii, 12].

paras.t: Sed præinductis objici potest, quia pro peccatis propriis in hac vita puniri, meritorium esse videtur, quum non puniat Deus bis in id ipsum, ut secundum antiquam translationem habetur apud Nahum prophetam, ubi nostra habet translatio: Non consurget duplex tribulatio. Alioqui pœnitentia seu emendatio in confessione injuncta, non esset satisfactoria ac meritoria: quum tamen omne quod ex caritate quis agit aut sustinet, meritorium asseratur. — Respondetur, quod secundum rigorem justitiæ, pati debitam pœnam pro propria culpa, non est meritorium, habendo respectum ad cohabitudinem pœnæ et culpæ inter se. Verumtamen, in quantum quis pœnam illam pro suis culpis sponte ex caritate cum contritione acceptat, ac sufferit ad Dei honorem, in illatæ ei injuriæ recompensam, meritorium perhibetur.
paras.en: But against what has been brought forward it may be objected that being punished in this life for one's own sins seems to be meritorious, since God does not punish twice for the same thing, as we have in the prophet Nahum according to the old translation [that is, the Old Latin, made from the Greek], where our translation has: [[Nah 1:9|there shall not rise a double affliction|Non consurget duplex tribulatio]]. Otherwise the penance or amendment enjoined in confession would not be satisfactory and meritorious; whereas everything that one does or endures out of charity is said to be meritorious. The answer is that, according to the rigour of justice, to suffer the punishment due for one's own fault is not meritorious, considering the relation of punishment and fault to each other. Nevertheless, in so far as someone accepts that punishment for his faults willingly, out of charity, with contrition, and bears it for the honour of God, in recompense for the injury done to Him, it is called meritorious.

paras.t: Quum itaque tam acceptum sit Deo, injurias absque propria culpa æquanimiter ferre, merito obediendum est etiam dyscolis dominis cum timore, quamvis nonnunquam molesti et injuriosi sint suis ministris. — Denique triplex est patientiæ gradus: primus, pro propriis culpis correptiones et correctiones patienter sufferre; secundus, absque propria culpa pati libenter adversa, non tamen pro justitia (sicut religiosi interdum a suis patribus corripiuntur, ut probentur, exerceantur, perfectique fiant); tertius, absque propria culpa pro justitia ea æquanimiter tolerare. Primus gradus est bonus: secundus, melior; tertius, optimus et perfectus.
paras.en: Since, then, it is so acceptable to God to bear injuries with equanimity without one's own fault, rightly are even froward masters to be obeyed with fear, although they are sometimes troublesome and injurious to their servants. Further, there are three degrees of patience: the first, to bear patiently reproofs and corrections for one's own faults; the second, to suffer adversities willingly without one's own fault, yet not for justice (as religious are sometimes reproved by their fathers so that they may be tried, exercised and made perfect); the third, to endure them with equanimity without one's own fault, for justice. The first degree is good, the second better, the third best and perfect.

paras.t: Consequenter exemplo Christi docet beatissimus Petrus patientiam plenam, et beneficia Christi commemorat. Quia et Christus passus est pro nobis, id est pro nostra salute, pro nostris peccatis delendis, pro gratia multiplici nobis promerenda, pro gloria nobis impertienda. Propter quod ait apud Joannem: Animam meam pono pro ovibus meis. Et per Isaiam loquitur Deus Pater: Propter scelus populi mei percussi eum. Vobis relinquens exemplum, ut sequamini vestigia ejus, id est, ejus intuitu et amore sustineatis libenter adversa, quoniam servi et membra suo capiti ac domino debent se conformare. Propter quod ipsemet ait: Qui vult venire post me, abneget semetipsum, et tollat crucem suam quotidie, et sequatur me; et rursus, Qui non bajulat crucem suam, et sequitur me, non est me dignus. Hinc ait Joannes apostolus: Qui se dicit in Christo manere, debet sicut ille ambulavit, et ipse ambulare. Quum dixisset S. Petrus, Christus passus est pro nobis, cur adjecit, Vobis, et non potius, Nobis, nisi forsitan ut exhortatio sua cordibus eorum quibus scripsit, fortius inculcaretur?
paras.en: Next, by the example of Christ, the most blessed Peter teaches full patience, and recalls the benefits of Christ. [[2:21|because Christ also suffered for us|Quia et Christus passus est pro nobis]], that is, for our salvation, for the blotting out of our sins, for meriting manifold grace for us, for bestowing glory on us. Wherefore he says in John: [[John 10:15|I lay down my life for my sheep|Animam meam pono pro ovibus meis]] [the margin gives Joann. v, 15]. And God the Father says through Isaias: [[Is 53:8|for the wickedness of my people have I struck him|Propter scelus populi mei percussi eum]]. [[2:21|leaving you an example that you should follow his steps|Vobis relinquens exemplum, ut sequamini vestigia ejus]], that is, that looking to him and for love of him you should willingly endure adversities, since servants and members ought to conform themselves to their head and lord. Wherefore he himself says: [[Luke 9:23|If any man will come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me|Qui vult venire post me, abneget semetipsum, et tollat crucem suam quotidie, et sequatur me]]; and again, [[Luke 14:27|doth not carry his cross|Qui non bajulat crucem suam]], [[Matt 10:38|and followeth me, is not worthy of me|et sequitur me, non est me dignus]]. Hence John the apostle says: [[1 John 2:6|He that saith he abideth in him ought himself also to walk even as he walked|Qui se dicit in Christo manere, debet sicut ille ambulavit, et ipse ambulare]]. When St. Peter had said, [[2:21|Christ also suffered for us|Christus passus est pro nobis]], why did he add, *you*, and not rather *us*, unless perhaps so that his exhortation might be more forcefully impressed on the hearts of those to whom he wrote?

paras.t: Qui peccatum non fecit, nec inventus est dolus in ore ejus. Hoc idem apud Isaiam scriptum est. Fuit enim Deus et homo, omniumque salvator: idcirco nequaquam decuit culpam esse in eo. Fuitque ejus humanitas ab incarnationis exordio perfectissime confirmata in bono.
paras.en: [[2:22|Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth.|Qui peccatum non fecit, nec inventus est dolus in ore ejus]] The same is written in Isaias[[Is 53:9||]]. For he was God and man, and the saviour of all: therefore it was in no way fitting that there should be fault in him. And his humanity was from the beginning of the incarnation most perfectly confirmed in good.

paras.t: Qui quum malediceretur a Judæis dicentibus, Blasphemavit, Reus est mortis, et, Crucifigatur, non maledicebat eis; quum pateretur, non comminabatur. Imo pro crucifixoribus suis oravit, et tanquam agnus coram tondente, obmutuit. Tradebat autem judicanti se injuste, id est, Pilato, qui ipsum injuste adjudicavit morti dirissimæ, permisit se tradi a Judæis. Imo et sponte ac libentissime ivit ad ipsum, ex ardentissima caritate et obedientia summa, qua pro nobis pati optavit prout Deus Pater disposuit. Ideo loquitur Isaias: Tradidit in mortem animam suam. Et ipsemet loquitur: Nemo tollit animam meam a me, sed ego pono eam.
paras.en: [[2:23|Who, when he was reviled|Qui quum malediceretur]] by the Jews, who said, [[Matt 26:65|He hath blasphemed|Blasphemavit]], [[Matt 26:66|He is guilty of death|Reus est mortis]], and, [[Matt 27:23|Let him be crucified|Crucifigatur]], [[2:23|did not revile|non maledicebat]] them; [[2:23|when he suffered, he threatened not|quum pateretur, non comminabatur]]. Nay, he prayed for his crucifiers[[Luke 23:34||]], and [[Is 53:7|as a lamb before his shearer|agnus coram tondente]] was dumb. [[2:23|but delivered himself to him that judged him unjustly|Tradebat autem judicanti se injuste]], that is, he allowed himself to be delivered by the Jews to Pilate, who unjustly sentenced him to a most dreadful death[[Luke 23:24||]][[Luke 23:25||]]. Nay, he went to him of his own accord and most willingly, out of most ardent charity and supreme obedience, by which he chose to suffer for us as God the Father disposed. Therefore Isaias says: [[Is 53:12|he hath delivered his soul unto death|Tradidit in mortem animam suam]]. And he himself says: [[John 10:18|No man taketh it away from me: but I lay it down|Nemo tollit animam meam a me, sed ego pono eam]].

paras.t: Qui peccata nostra ipse pertulit in corpore suo super lignum, id est, pœnam amarissimam pro nostris peccatis in cruce sustinuit, in proprio corpore immaculatissimo, tenerrime ac nobilissime complexionato, ideoque maxime perceptivo doloris, et summe passivo. Hoc est quod loquitur Isaias: Vere languores nostros ipse tulit, et dolores nostros ipse portavit; et Deus posuit in eo iniquitatem omnium nostrum. Ut peccatis mortui, id est a vitiis expurgati, justitiæ vivamus, id est, virtuosis actibus simus intenti ac subditi, et Christo, qui est justitia vera, in omnibus obsequamur. Ipse enim factus est nobis a Deo justitia, et sanctificatio, et redemptio, ut asserit Paulus. De quo et per Isaiam loquitur Dominus: Prope est justitia mea ut reveletur. Cujus livore sanati sumus (* estis) a vitiis, quæ sunt animarum infirmitates.
paras.en: [[2:24|Who his own self bore our sins in his body upon the tree|Qui peccata nostra ipse pertulit in corpore suo super lignum]], that is, he bore most bitter punishment for our sins on the cross, in his own most immaculate body, most tenderly and nobly constituted [that is, of the most delicate bodily temperament], and therefore most sensitive to pain and supremely capable of suffering. This is what Isaias says: [[Is 53:4|Surely he hath borne our infirmities and carried our sorrows|Vere languores nostros ipse tulit, et dolores nostros ipse portavit]]; and [[Is 53:6|the Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all|Deus posuit in eo iniquitatem omnium nostrum]] [Denis has *Deus*, God, for the Vulgate's *Dominus*]. [[2:24|that we, being dead to sins|Ut peccatis mortui]], that is, purged of vices, [[2:24|should live to justice|justitiæ vivamus]], that is, may be intent on and subject to virtuous acts, and may obey in all things Christ, who is true justice. For he [[1 Cor 1:30|who of God is made unto us|factus est nobis a Deo]] [[1 Cor 1:30|justice and sanctification and redemption|justitia, et sanctificatio, et redemptio]], as Paul declares. Of him too the Lord says through Isaias: Near is [[Is 56:1|my justice to be revealed|justitia mea ut reveletur]] [the margin gives Is. lxi, 1; the words are those of Is 56:1, with *Prope est*, "is near", as in Is 51:5]. [[2:24|by whose stripes you were healed|Cujus livore sanati sumus]] [Denis reads *sumus*, "we were"; the asterisk in the print gives the Vulgate's *estis*, "you were"] from vices, which are the infirmities of souls.

paras.t: Eratis enim aliquando sicut oves errantes, scilicet ante conversionem vestram ad Christum. Omnia verba ista quasi ex Isaia sumpta sunt. Ubi et legitur: Omnes nos quasi oves erravimus; unusquisque in viam suam declinavit. Psalmista quoque: Erravi, inquit, sicut ovis quæ periit. Sed conversi estis nunc ad pastorem et episcopum animarum vestrarum, id est ad Christum, qui multiplici alimento animas vestras alit ac roborat, videlicet proprio corpore et sanguine, pane bonæ operationis, pane lacrimarum et compunctionis, refectione contemplationis, dulcedine interna consolationis.
paras.en: [[2:25|For you were|Eratis enim]] at one time [[2:25|as sheep going astray|sicut oves errantes]], namely before your conversion to Christ. All these words are as it were taken from Isaias, where we also read: [[Is 53:6|All we like sheep have gone astray, every one hath turned aside into his own way|Omnes nos quasi oves erravimus; unusquisque in viam suam declinavit]]. The Psalmist too: [[Ps 118:176|I have gone astray|Erravi]], he says, [[Ps 118:176|like a sheep that is lost|sicut ovis quæ periit]]. [[2:25|but you are now converted to the shepherd and bishop of your souls|Sed conversi estis nunc ad pastorem et episcopum animarum vestrarum]], that is, to Christ, who feeds and strengthens your souls with manifold nourishment: namely with his own body and blood, with the bread of good works, the bread of tears and compunction, the refreshment of contemplation, the inward sweetness of consolation.

paras.t: Qui etiam episcopus animarum vocatur, id est earum saluti intentus, seu superintentor salutis earum. Episcopus quippe superintendens interpretatur: ab ἐπί, quod est supra, et […] intentio. Alia littera habet, Ad pastorem et visitatorem animarum vestrarum. Nam Christus visitavit nos oriens ex alto. Qui et quotidie visitat animas electorum luce gratiæ ac miserationum suarum. Ipse quoque Salvator est rex et pontifex noster, advocatus interpellans pro nobis. De quo ad Hebræos fertur: Christus eo quod maneat in æternum, sempiternum habet sacerdotium: unde et salvare potest in perpetuum, accedens per semetipsum ad Deum, semper vivens ad interpellandum pro nobis.
paras.en: He is also called the *bishop* of souls, that is, one intent on their salvation, or the overseer of their salvation. For *bishop* is interpreted "superintending": from ἐπί, which means "over", and […], "attention" [the lost Greek word is presumably σκοπός or σκοπεῖν, "watcher", "to watch"]. Another reading has: To the shepherd and visitor of your souls. For Christ, [[Luke 1:78|the Orient from on high hath visited us|visitavit nos oriens ex alto]]; and he daily visits the souls of the elect with the light of his grace and mercies. The Saviour himself is also our king and high priest, our advocate interceding for us[[Rom 8:34||]]. Of him it is said to the Hebrews: Christ, [[Heb 7:24|for that he continueth for ever, hath an everlasting priesthood|eo quod maneat in æternum, sempiternum habet sacerdotium]]: [[Heb 7:25|Whereby he is able also to save for ever|unde et salvare potest in perpetuum]], drawing near through himself to God [Denis reads *accedens*, "drawing near", of Christ himself; the Vulgate has *accedentes*, "them that come"], [[Heb 7:25|always living to make intercession for us|semper vivens ad interpellandum pro nobis]].

3.title: PROSECUTIO EXPOSITIONIS HUJUS CAPITULI TERTII, AB EO LOCO: ET QUIS EST QUI VOBIS NOCEAT?
3.title_en: Continuation of the exposition of this third chapter, from the place: And who is he that can hurt you?

paras.t: ABUNDAVIT in primitiva Ecclesia Christianorum persecutio copiosa, ferox, assidua. Idcirco conversi ad fidem, indigebant confortatione et informatione ad patientiam. Et hoc nunc agit Apostolorum dignissimus vertex. Et quis est qui vobis noceat, si boni æmulatores fueritis? Tanquam dicat: Nullus vobis potest nocere, si æmulatores, hoc est amatores seu imitatores, estis boni, hoc est Dei seu Christi essentialiter boni; vel, Boni, id est virtutis. Nam qui hujusmodi boni est æmulator, non dejicitur per adversa, sed Deo firmiter est inhærens. Idcirco tribulatio cooperatur ei in meritorum augmentum; et si lædatur in corpore, si spolietur substantia, si diffametur, non ei hæc nocent, sed mirabiliter prosunt, si ea æquanimiter ferat, quemadmodum ægro non nocet amara potio, sectio sive adustio. Ideo dictum est: Nulla nocebit adversitas, si nulla dominetur iniquitas. Eis vero qui inferunt ista justis, maxime nocet horum illatio, quum peccent mortaliter. Uniuscujusque siquidem malum in proprium redundat auctorem. Et cui hæc nocent, ex propria impatientia, ira, seu alia culpa nocent. Ideo in Ecclesiaste dicitur: Qui fodit foveam, incidet in eam; et qui dissipat sepem, mordebit eum coluber.
paras.en: In the primitive Church the persecution of Christians abounded, plentiful, fierce and unceasing. Therefore those converted to the faith needed strengthening and instruction in patience. And this the most worthy head of the Apostles now does. [[3:13|And who is he that can hurt you, if you be zealous of good?|Et quis est qui vobis noceat, si boni æmulatores fueritis?]] As if he said: No one can hurt you, if you are zealous, that is, lovers or imitators, of the good, that is, of God or Christ, who is essentially good; or, *of good*, that is, of virtue. For he who is zealous of such good is not cast down by adversity, but cleaves firmly to God. Therefore tribulation works together for him unto the increase of merits; and if he be hurt in body, if he be stripped of his substance, if he be defamed, these things do not hurt him but wonderfully profit him, if he bear them with equanimity, just as a bitter draught, cutting or cautery does not hurt a sick man. Hence it has been said: No adversity shall hurt, if no iniquity have dominion. But to those who inflict these things on the just, the inflicting of them does the greatest hurt, since they sin mortally. For each man's evil rebounds upon its own author. And those whom these things hurt, they hurt through their own impatience, anger or other fault. Therefore it is said in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 10:8|He that diggeth a pit, shall fall into it: and he that breaketh a hedge, a serpent shall bite him|Qui fodit foveam, incidet in eam; et qui dissipat sepem, mordebit eum coluber]].

paras.t: Sed his objici potest, quoniam, ut videtur, impiissimi hæresiarchæ valde nocuerunt multis bonis Catholicis, quorum fidem pestiferis persuasionibus everterunt. Nonne sacrilegus et damnatissimus Arius totum pene orbem infecit? Unde et Beda hic ait: Constat plurimos boni æmulatores, læsos esse ab aliis, dum in veritatis, quam diligunt, cognitione male instructi sunt. Quantos enim in Deum catholice credere et recte in Ecclesia vivere cupientes, Arii vesania, quantos Sabellii aliorumque hæreticorum nequitia nescientes seduxit? Lege Joannis Chrysostomi librum quem scripsit de eo, videlicet, Neminem posse lædi ab alio, nisi a semetipso. Hæc Beda. Verum de isto longa posset disputatio introduci. Sed brevitati studendum est, et breviter respondendum, quod sicut diabolus tentando inclinat, non compellit, homines ad peccata, ipsi vero libere consentiendo tentanti, se ipsos præcipitant: sic hæresiarchæ potuerunt inclinare, non cogere, ad errores; nec persecutores, absolute loquendo, compulerunt fideles ad sacrificandum, sed qui sacrificaverunt ex pœnis inducti, ex propria infirmitate et imperfectione cesserunt et perierunt. Hinc subditur:
paras.en: But against this it may be objected that, as it seems, the most impious heresiarchs greatly hurt many good Catholics, whose faith they overthrew by pestilent persuasions. Did not the sacrilegious and most damned Arius infect almost the whole world? Hence Bede too says here: It is certain that very many zealous of good have been hurt by others, while they were badly instructed in the knowledge of the truth which they love. For how many who desired to believe in God in the Catholic way and to live rightly in the Church did the madness of Arius, how many did the wickedness of Sabellius and other heretics seduce unawares? Read the book of John Chrysostom which he wrote on this, namely, That no one can be hurt by another, except by himself. Thus Bede. Truly a long disputation could be brought in on this. But brevity must be studied, and the brief answer is that, just as the devil by tempting inclines men to sin but does not compel them, while they, freely consenting to the tempter, cast themselves headlong: so the heresiarchs could incline men to errors, not force them; nor did the persecutors, speaking absolutely, compel the faithful to sacrifice, but those who sacrificed, induced by punishments, gave way and perished through their own weakness and imperfection. Hence it is added:

paras.t: Sed et si quid patimini propter justitiam, beati estis nunc in merito et spe, beati futuri in præmio et re: sicut ait Salvator, Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam, quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum. Et rursus, loquens diffusius, et justos plenissime recreans ac consolans, ait ibidem: Beati estis quum maledixerint vobis homines, et persecuti vos fuerint, et dixerint omne malum adversum vos, mentientes, propter me; gaudete in illa hora et exsultate, quoniam merces vestra copiosa est in cœlis. Patiendo namque æquanimiter aspera propter justitiam, purgamur a culpis, implemur potioribus gratiæ donis, Christo assimilamur, a futuris eripimur pœnis, propinquamus ad regnum, et gloriæ promeremur augmentum. Denique, qui correptionem et correctionem pro suis peccatis gratanter suscipiunt, ut in vita præsenti purgentur ac Deo complaceant, quamvis pro suis patiantur demeritis, tamen aliquo modo, puta finaliter, propter justitiam pati dicuntur, et reputatur eis hoc ipsum ad meritum, suntque beati. Miseri vero sunt, et miseri vehementer, qui corripi ac corrigi dedignantur.
paras.en: [[3:14|But if also you suffer any thing for justice' sake, blessed are ye|Sed et si quid patimini propter justitiam, beati]] now in merit and hope, to be blessed hereafter in reward and in reality: as the Saviour says, [[Matt 5:10|Blessed are they that suffer persecution for justice' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven|Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam, quoniam ipsorum est regnum cœlorum]]. And again, speaking more at length, and most fully refreshing and consoling the just, he says in the same place: [[Matt 5:11|Blessed are ye when they shall revile you, and persecute you, and speak all that is evil against you, untruly, for my sake|Beati estis quum maledixerint vobis homines, et persecuti vos fuerint, et dixerint omne malum adversum vos, mentientes, propter me]]; [[Matt 5:12|Be glad and rejoice for your reward is very great in heaven|gaudete in illa hora et exsultate, quoniam merces vestra copiosa est in cœlis]] [Denis reads “rejoice in that hour”]. For by suffering harsh things with equanimity for justice' sake, we are purged of faults, filled with greater gifts of grace, made like to Christ, delivered from future punishments; we draw near to the kingdom and merit an increase of glory. Finally, those who gladly accept reproof and correction for their sins, that they may be purged in the present life and please God, although they suffer for their own demerits, are yet in some manner, namely as to their end [that is, in the purpose for which they accept it], said to suffer for justice' sake; and this very thing is reckoned to them for merit, and they are blessed. But wretched, and exceedingly wretched, are those who disdain to be reproved and corrected.

paras.t: Timorem autem, id est causam timoris, videlicet crudelitatem et persecutionem, eorum qui adversa infligunt, ne timueritis, immoderato timore a virtutum constantia retrahente. Ideo subditur: ut non conturbemini, id est, ne ordinationem rationis tranquillitatemque mentis perdatis, et ita aliorum pravitate vincamini. Hinc jubet Salvator: Nolite timere eos qui corpus occidunt. Et in Proverbiis habetur: Justus quasi leo confidens, absque terrore erit; et in Isaia, Quis tu, ut timeas ab homine mortali, et a filio hominis, qui quasi fœnum arescit? Verumtamen timor adversitatum et mortis, naturalis dumtaxat, excusatur a culpa, quum et Christus timuerit mortem ex prævio rationis judicio. Aliqui vero timent se formidaturos tribulatione instante: qui quod evadere cupiunt, ante tempus assumunt. Quibus consulitur ut Dominum deprecentur, quatenus eos ab omni inordinato expurget pavore, cum Psalmista orantes, A timore inimici eripe animam meam: non ut me non occidat inimicus, sed ut non timeam occidentem inimicum. Considerent etiam quam salubre sit pati adversa, quamque proficuum, et quam brevis sit omnis tribulatio vitæ præsentis, et quanta sustinuerunt Christus et Sancti. Ex quorum omnium intuitione constantes ac fortes, imo et læti sint in tribulationibus et tormentis.
paras.en: [[3:14|And be not afraid of their fear|Timorem autem eorum ne timueritis]]: *their fear*, that is, the cause of fear, namely the cruelty and persecution of those who inflict adversities; be not afraid with an immoderate fear that draws you back from constancy in the virtues. Therefore he adds: [[3:14|and be not troubled|ut non conturbemini]], that is, lest you lose the ordering of reason and tranquillity of mind, and so be overcome by the depravity of others. Hence the Saviour commands: [[Matt 10:28|fear ye not them that kill the body|Nolite timere eos qui corpus occidunt]]. And in Proverbs we have: [[Prov 28:1|the just, bold as a lion, shall be without dread|Justus quasi leo confidens, absque terrore erit]]; and in Isaias: [[Is 51:12|who art thou, that thou shouldst be afraid of a mortal man, and of the son of man, who shall wither away like grass?|Quis tu, ut timeas ab homine mortali, et a filio hominis, qui quasi fœnum arescit?]]? Nevertheless fear of adversities and of death, when it is merely natural, is excused from fault, since Christ too feared death with the prior judgment of reason[[Matt 26:38||]]. But some fear that they will be terrified when tribulation comes: these take up beforehand what they wish to escape. They are counselled to beseech the Lord to purge them of all inordinate dread, praying with the Psalmist: [[Ps 63:2|deliver my soul from the fear of the enemy|A timore inimici eripe animam meam]]: not that the enemy may not kill me, but that I may not fear the enemy who kills. Let them consider also how wholesome it is to suffer adversity, and how profitable, and how brief is all the tribulation of the present life, and how much Christ and the Saints endured. From the contemplation of all these let them be constant and strong, nay even joyful, in tribulations and torments.

paras.t: Dominum autem Christum sanctificate, id est, magnifice honorate, firmiterque tenete, et sanctum esse sentite, in cordibus vestris, videlicet in intellectu et voluntate, eum sinceriter contemplando, fervide diligendo, et totis viribus honorando. Juxta hunc sensum oramus assidue: Pater noster, qui es in cœlis, sanctificetur nomen tuum. Et Propheta hortatur: Magnificate Dominum mecum. Per Ezechielem quoque Dominus fatur: Quum sanctificatus fuero in vobis. Et Isaias ait: Dominum exercituum sanctificate.
paras.en: [[3:15|But sanctify the Lord Christ|Dominum autem Christum sanctificate]], that is, honour him magnificently, hold him firmly, and acknowledge him to be holy, [[3:15|in your hearts|in cordibus vestris]], namely in understanding and will, by contemplating him sincerely, loving him fervently, and honouring him with all your strength. In this sense we pray continually: [[Matt 6:9|Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name|Pater noster, qui es in cœlis, sanctificetur nomen tuum]]. And the Prophet exhorts: [[Ps 33:4|O magnify the Lord with me|Magnificate Dominum mecum]] [the margin gives Ps. xxxiii, 3; in the Vulgate numbering the words are at 33:4]. Through Ezechiel too the Lord speaks: [[Ezech 36:23|when I shall be sanctified in you|Quum sanctificatus fuero in vobis]]. And Isaias says: [[Is 8:13|Sanctify the Lord of hosts|Dominum exercituum sanctificate]].

paras.t: Parati semper ad satisfactionem omni poscenti vos rationem de ea quæ in vobis est, fide et spe, id est, tam instructi et sapientes in evangelica lege sitis, ut jugiter prompti sitis ad dandam rationabilem responsionem et causam universis a vobis quærentibus rationes fidei vestræ ac spei: cur scilicet tam incomprehensibilia credatis, tamque supernaturalem beatitudinem, et secreta ac invisibilia bona adipisci speretis.
paras.en: [[3:15|being ready always to satisfy every one that asketh you a reason of that hope which is in you|Parati semper ad satisfactionem omni poscenti vos rationem de ea quæ in vobis est]], [Denis's text reads “faith and hope”] that is, be so instructed and wise in the law of the Gospel that you are continually ready to give a reasonable answer and ground to all who ask of you the reasons of your faith and hope: namely why you believe things so incomprehensible, and hope to obtain so supernatural a beatitude and goods so secret and invisible.

paras.t: Potest autem quis rationem fidei ac spei interrogare a Christiano dupliciter: primo, fideliter; secundo, infideliter. Qui fideliter quærit, caritative informandus est, et potest faciliter contentari. Qui vero infideliter sciscitatur, non ita faciliter contentatur; sed opponit et arguit quousque vincatur. Utrisque tamen eædem rationes fidei ac spei sunt assignandæ, quod scilicet ita credimus et speramus: quoniam Deus altissimus, omnipotens, verax, qui nec fallere potest nec falli, huic nostræ fidei et spei testimonium perhibuit, primo per Christum, deinde per sanctos Apostolos ceterosque Christi discipulos et viros sanctos, imo per utriusque sexus personas innumerabiles, usque in præsens, per innumera et præclara miracula soli omnipotentiæ suæ possibilia: quæ partim in Scripturis canonicis sunt descripta, partim in chronicis, aliisque historiis et legendis authenticis. Secundo, quoniam quidquid de Christo credimus et speramus in evangelicæ legis Scripturis, in veteris Testamenti Scripturis per Moysen et beatos Prophetas copiose legimus prophetatum. Tertio, quia lex Christi, est lex totius sanctitatis et honestatis ac perfectionis. Quarto, per finalem istam Judæorum relictionem probamus Christum venisse. Quinto, ostenditur veritas fidei per hoc, quod quanto adversarii et tyranni atrocius nitebantur fidem christianam prorsus exstinguere, tanto plus crevit atque invaluit. Ex quibus omnibus, multisque aliis rationibus, sufficienter et certe probatur, quod fidei nostræ ac spei Deus sit auctor ac testis: quamvis per ea fidei veritates supernaturales ita probari non queant ut comprehendantur per rationem, certitudinemque evidentiæ habeant.
paras.en: Now a man may ask a Christian the reason of his faith and hope in two ways: first, faithfully; second, unfaithfully. He who asks faithfully is to be instructed charitably, and can easily be satisfied. But he who inquires unfaithfully is not so easily satisfied, but objects and argues until he is overcome. To both, however, the same reasons of faith and hope are to be given, namely why we so believe and hope: first, because the most high God, almighty and true, who can neither deceive nor be deceived, has borne witness to this our faith and hope, first through Christ, then through the holy Apostles and the other disciples of Christ and holy men, nay through innumerable persons of either sex down to the present, by countless and glorious miracles possible to his omnipotence alone: which are recorded partly in the canonical Scriptures, partly in chronicles and other authentic histories and legends. Second, because whatever we believe and hope concerning Christ in the Scriptures of the Gospel law, we read abundantly prophesied in the Scriptures of the Old Testament through Moses and the blessed Prophets. Third, because the law of Christ is a law of all holiness, uprightness and perfection. Fourth, by this final abandonment of the Jews we prove that Christ has come. Fifth, the truth of the faith is shown by this, that the more fiercely adversaries and tyrants strove utterly to extinguish the Christian faith, the more it grew and prevailed. From all these and many other reasons it is sufficiently and certainly proved that God is the author and witness of our faith and hope: although by them the supernatural truths of faith cannot be so proved as to be comprehended by reason and to have the certitude of evidence.

paras.t: Verumtamen, fidem contra adversariorum disputationem defendere, et eam diversis argumentationibus rationabiliter persuadere ac declarare, non est omnium, sed specialiter eruditorum. Nec est præceptum ut unusquisque fidelis paratus sit ad satisfaciendum quærentibus rationem fidei ac spei, quum multi sint idiotæ et penitus simplices; sed istud est magis consilium. Prælati tamen et superiores atque doctores, seu prædicatores, tenentur aliquo modo esse parati ad satisfactionem hujusmodi, quum apud Malachiam dicatur: Labia sacerdotis custodiunt scientiam, et legem requirent de ore ejus, quia angelus Domini exercituum est. In primitiva quoque Ecclesia, præparatio et eruditio ista ad satisfactionem talem magis necessaria fuit, quam nunc: quia tunc fideles inter perfidos undique morabantur, et sæpe inde interrogabantur, etiam a tyrannis. Fuitque eis necesse fidem contra adversarios ejus defendere.
paras.en: Nevertheless, to defend the faith against the disputing of adversaries, and to commend and set it forth reasonably by various arguments, is not for all, but especially for the learned. Nor is it a precept that every one of the faithful be ready to satisfy those who ask the reason of faith and hope, since many are unlettered and wholly simple; rather this is a counsel [that is, advice of perfection, not a binding command]. Prelates, however, and superiors and doctors or preachers are bound in some manner to be ready for such satisfaction, since it is said in Malachias: [[Mal 2:7|the lips of the priests shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law at his mouth: because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts|Labia sacerdotis custodiunt scientiam, et legem requirent de ore ejus, quia angelus Domini exercituum est]]. In the primitive Church, too, this preparation and learning for such satisfaction was more necessary than now: because then the faithful dwelt everywhere among unbelievers, and were often questioned on this, even by tyrants; and it was necessary for them to defend the faith against its adversaries.

paras.t: Sed cum modestia et timore, id est, postulantibus a vobis rationem fidei vestræ ac spei, respondete modeste et timorate, humiliter et decenter, ne interrogatores scandalizentur in vobis, et se despici arbitrantes, contra fidem et ejus professores gravius accendantur. Hinc ad Romanos loquitur Paulus: Infirmum in fide assumite, non in disceptationibus cogitationum. Timotheo quoque scribens: Noli, inquit, verbis contendere: ad nihil enim utile est, nisi ad subversionem audientium. Itemque: Servum Domini non oportet litigare, sed patientem esse, et cum modestia corripientem eos qui resistunt. Denique, quum ea quæ fidei sunt, sint tam sublimia, incomprehensibilissima ac profunda, non nisi cum casto Dei timore de eis loqui et disputare debemus, ne forsitan Dominum offendamus, irreverenter et præsumptuose loquendo de ipso et mysteriis ejus: quia ut in Proverbiis asseritur, Sicut qui mel comedit multum, non est ei bonum, sic qui perscrutator est majestatis, opprimetur a gloria. Propter quod, ut divinus Dionysius et Damascenus affirmant, non est audendum aliquid dicere de superessentiali Deitate, præter ea quæ nobis sunt in sacris eloquiis tradita. Conscientiam habentes bonam, ita ut vobis non sitis conscii de aliqua simulatione, nequitia aut culpa occulta, quemadmodum ad Corinthios asserit Paulus: Gloria nostra hæc est, testimonium conscientiæ nostræ, quod in simplicitate et sinceritate Dei, non in sapientia carnali, conversati sumus in hoc mundo.
paras.en: [[3:16|But with modesty and fear|Sed cum modestia et timore]], that is, to those who ask of you the reason of your faith and hope, answer modestly and with fear, humbly and becomingly, lest the questioners be scandalized in you and, thinking themselves despised, be more grievously inflamed against the faith and its professors. Hence Paul says to the Romans: [[Rom 14:1|him that is weak in faith, take unto you: not in disputes about thoughts|Infirmum in fide assumite, non in disceptationibus cogitationum]]. And writing to Timothy: [[2 Tim 2:14|Contend not in words: for it is to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers|Noli … verbis contendere … subversionem audientium]]. And again: [[2 Tim 2:24|the servant of the Lord must not wrangle|Servum Domini non oportet litigare]], but be patient, [[2 Tim 2:25|With modesty admonishing them that resist|cum modestia corripientem eos qui resistunt]]. Finally, since the things of faith are so sublime, so utterly incomprehensible and profound, we ought not to speak and dispute of them except with the chaste fear of God, lest perhaps we offend the Lord by speaking irreverently and presumptuously of him and his mysteries: for, as is said in Proverbs, [[Prov 25:27|As it is not good for a man to eat much honey, so he that is a searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory|Sicut qui mel comedit multum, non est ei bonum, sic qui perscrutator est majestatis, opprimetur a gloria]]. Wherefore, as the divine Dionysius and Damascene affirm, we must not dare to say anything of the superessential Deity beyond what is handed down to us in the sacred oracles. [[3:16|having a good conscience|Conscientiam habentes bonam]], so that you are not conscious to yourselves of any pretence, wickedness or hidden fault, as Paul asserts to the Corinthians: [[2 Cor 1:12|our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity of heart and sincerity of God, and not in carnal wisdom|Gloria nostra hæc est, testimonium conscientiæ nostræ, quod in simplicitate et sinceritate Dei, non in sapientia carnali]], we have conversed in this world.

paras.t: Ut in eo quod detrahunt de vobis, confundantur qui calumniantur vestram bonam conversationem, id est, detractores vestri, vobis incaute obloquentes, ex vestra rationabili responsione quam eis assignatis de fide et spe vestra, atque ex sancta vita vestra, confundantur, ipsa evidentia veritatis ac virtutis convicti, aut etiam tandem conversi. Vel, Confundantur in die judicii, quando justi stabunt in magna constantia adversus persecutores, irrisores, detractoresque suos. Unde per Jeremiam ait vir justus: Confundantur qui persequuntur me, et non confundar ego; paveant illi, et non paveam ego: induc super eos diem afflictionis. Hinc ad Titum habetur: Verbum sanum sit et irreprehensibile, ut is qui ex adverso est, vereatur, nihil mali habens loqui de vobis.
paras.en: [[3:16|that whereas they speak evil of you, they may be ashamed who falsely accuse your good conversation|Ut in eo quod detrahunt de vobis, confundantur qui calumniantur vestram bonam conversationem]], that is, your detractors, who rashly speak against you, may be confounded by the reasonable answer you give them about your faith and hope, and by your holy life, being convicted by the very evidence of truth and virtue, or even at length converted. Or: may be confounded at the day of judgment, when the just shall stand with great constancy against their persecutors, mockers and detractors[[Wis 5:1||]]. Hence through Jeremias the just man says: [[Jer 17:18|Let them be confounded that persecute me, and let not me be confounded: let them be afraid, and let not me be afraid: bring upon them the day of affliction|Confundantur qui persequuntur me, et non confundar ego; paveant illi, et non paveam ego: induc super eos diem afflictionis]]. Hence we have in the Epistle to Titus: [[Tit 2:8|The sound word that can not be blamed: that he who is on the contrary part may be afraid, having no evil to say|Verbum sanum sit et irreprehensibile, ut is qui ex adverso est, vereatur, nihil mali habens loqui]] of you.

paras.t: Hæc igitur agite cum bona conscientia, nec ex timore persecutionum omittite ea. Melius est enim, id est magis laudabile, magisque meritorium, benefacientes si velit voluntas Dei pati adversa, quam malefacientes: hoc est, virtuosius fuerit ut absque demerito vestro, utpote bene viventes, sustineatis adversa, quam ut ea pro vestris demeritis sustineatis, utpote male viventes: quemadmodum Job et Tobias amplius commendantur pro eo quod tanta perpessi sunt non pro suis excessibus, sed pro sua exercitatione et coronatione gloriosiori, atque ut aliis in exempla patientiæ ponerentur, quam Elymas magus et Joram, qui pro suis criminibus sunt plagati. Hac quoque auctoritate, secundum Bedam, reprehenditur eorum stultitia qui æquanimiter ferunt correptionem et correctionem quando culpabiles sunt, si vero absque culpa sua patiantur adversa aut arguantur, ægre accipiunt: et qui hactenus videbantur innoxii, per propriam iram, impatientiam, murmurationem, se noxios reddunt.
paras.en: Do these things, then, with a good conscience, and do not omit them for fear of persecutions. [[3:17|For it is better|Melius est enim]], that is, more praiseworthy and more meritorious, [[3:17|doing well (if such be the will of God) to suffer than doing ill|benefacientes si velit voluntas Dei pati adversa, quam malefacientes]] [Denis's text: “if the will of God will it, to suffer adversities”]: that is, it is more virtuous that you should endure adversities without demerit of your own, as living well, than that you should endure them for your demerits, as living ill: just as Job and Tobias are more commended because they suffered such things not for their own excesses, but for their exercise and more glorious crowning, and that they might be set as examples of patience to others[[Tob 2:12||]], than Elymas the magician[[Acts 13:8||]] and Joram[[2 Par 21:12||]], who were struck for their crimes.
